<p><b class=\"tm-rest\">La respiration</:
Breathing is done normally. This is the most misunderstood point: it is not about loading up on oxygen. The blood is already saturated at rest, and little can be added. Breathe calmly, from the belly, without forcing the amplitude.

Hyperventilation must be avoided. Blowing hard and fast before a hold drops carbon dioxide and artificially delays the urge to breathe. The hold feels easier, but oxygen depletes at the same rate. This is precisely the mechanism behind blackouts with no warning signs.

The final inhale is taken without excess, around eighty per cent of your capacity. A chest inflated to bursting creates tension that is paid for in early contractions.

During the hold, do not move. Every movement consumes. The body lets go in three stages: first the calm, then the first contractions of the diaphragm, then their intensification. Contractions are normal and expected; they signal no immediate danger — they mark the start of the useful work.
<p>Assure-toi d'être connecté au même co:
Make sure you are signed in to the same account on both, then run a manual sync from Settings.

Syncing runs in the background after each change, but it needs a network. Offline, everything stays saved on the device and goes up when you reconnect.
<p>C'est exact et c'est une limite du na:

<p>Choisis un moment où tu n'as rien der:
Pick a moment with nothing scheduled after. A table takes twenty to thirty minutes, and finishing in a rush defeats the purpose.

Stomach fairly empty: allow two to three hours after a full meal. Digestion in progress raises oxygen consumption and shortens everything.

No coffee in the preceding hour, no hard effort in the preceding two. Lie down, or settle with your back supported, and give your heart rate five minutes to come down before starting the timer.

Cold, noise, tight clothing at the waist: anything that draws attention costs seconds.
<p>L'envie de respirer ne vient pas du m:
The urge to breathe does not come from lack of oxygen but from the build-up of carbon dioxide. These are two distinct signals, and each table works on one of them.

The CO₂ table keeps holds at a constant length and shortens the rests. The carbon dioxide no longer has time to clear, so each hold starts from a higher level than the last. You never go far in duration, but you spend a lot of time in discomfort. This is tolerance training: learning to stay settled when the body demands.

The O₂ table does the opposite. The rests stay long and identical, the holds lengthen progressively. Each repetition dips a little lower in oxygen than the one before. This is adaptation training: the body learns to function on less.

A CO₂ table feels harder at the time; an O₂ table leaves you more tired afterwards. That is not just an impression.
<p>La table <b>CO₂</b> garde des apnées:
The CO₂ table keeps holds at a constant length and shortens the rests. You learn to tolerate the urge to breathe.

The O₂ table keeps rests constant and lengthens the holds. You learn to function on less oxygen.

The full detail is in the training guide, under Settings.
<p>Le max sert de base de calcul à toute:
The max is the basis for calculating all your tables: distort it and you distort everything else. Take a value reached comfortably, not a record wrung out on a good day.

Test it rarely, once a month at most. A max test is a session in its own right; it is not added to a table.

If it jumps by more than twenty per cent at once, be wary: that is often the sign of unintentional hyperventilation rather than a real gain.

And a max that stalls for weeks is entirely normal. Tolerance improves before duration does, and that does not show on the clock.
<p>Les exercices de l'onglet Souffle ne:
The exercises in the Breath tab do not replace the tables and do not substitute for them in your progression. They work on something else: regulating the nervous system, the quality of release, the habit of breathing through the nose.

Box breathing is the way in, and it comes in three levels. The open box removes the empty-lung hold, the one that most often blocks beginners. The classic box restores the four equal counts. The progressive box lengthens the side as the session goes on, which makes it the closest to genuine tolerance work.

They sit well on days without a table, or just before one to arrive settled. Buteyko is the closest to carbon dioxide tolerance work; NSDR serves recovery.

That is why they have no progress curve: there is nothing to beat.
<p>Les tables se pratiquent <b>exclusive:
Tables are practised strictly dry, lying down or seated, never in water nor at the edge of a pool. A blackout on dry land makes you fall; in water, it drowns you.

No hyperventilation before the hold. Dizziness, tingling or disturbed vision call for an immediate stop.

In case of heart or respiratory conditions, high blood pressure, epilepsy or pregnancy, seek medical advice before starting.
<p>Prends une durée que tu tiens confort:
Take a duration you hold comfortably, not a record wrung out on a good day. All your tables derive from it: an overestimated max produces needlessly hard tables, and you will spend your time interrupting them.

The Max test mode on the Tables screen lets you measure it. Once a month is ample.
<p>Trois leviers, dans cet ordre. Baisse:
Three levers, in this order. Lower the difficulty at creation: easy cuts the hold to 40 % of your max on CO₂, and the final hold to 65 % on O₂.

Then check your reference max: that is the most common cause. It easily varies by twenty per cent depending on sleep, stress and digestion.

Finally, a table is interrupted. The stop button is not a failure, it is the correct behaviour.
<p>Une séance interrompue est conservée:
An interrupted session is kept for six hours: a Resume banner appears at the top of the Tables screen. The current phase restarts from its beginning, never from the middle.

After six hours, it is discarded.
<p>Une table par séance, jamais deux. En:
One table per session, never two. Chaining a CO₂ and an O₂ in the same session stacks both fatigues with no added benefit.

Two to three sessions a week are ample to progress. Beyond that, recovery becomes the limiting factor and gains flatten out.

Alternate the types rather than piling them up: a CO₂, a rest day, an O₂. If you had to keep only one, the CO₂ is the one that pays off fastest, because tolerance to discomfort improves more quickly than physiological adaptation.

Tables sit badly right after a heavy training session. Put them in the morning, or on a light day.
<p>Une table s'interrompt, elle ne se fo:
A table is interrupted, not forced. The stop button is there for that, and using it is not a failure: it is the correct behaviour.

You stop immediately, without debate, at any of these signs: dizziness, tingling in the hands or lips, disturbed vision, a rising sensation of heat, contractions that have become unmanageable, or losing track of what you are doing.

After an interrupted hold, take full breaths and allow the complete recovery time before deciding whether to continue. Cutting the recovery short to catch up with the programme is the surest way to turn a failed session into a dangerous one.

If you have had to stop three holds in a row, the table is too hard for today. This is not a matter of willpower: your max on any given day depends on sleep, stress and digestion, and it easily varies by twenty per cent.
<p>Vérifie que le mode silencieux de l'a:
Check that the device's silent mode is off, then the Sound cues and Voice announcements settings.

Speech synthesis needs a gesture from you to start: if you turn the voice on while a session is already running, it will only take effect from the next session.

Keep the screen on during the session. In the web version, sound is not guaranteed once the screen is locked.
